opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it at a few levels.

The most basic one is that safety training is a fairly thin layer on top of a much larger base of capabilities. Pretraining gives the model a huge, general ability to continue text in almost any style or persona. Fine-tuning and RLHF then teach it a set of preferences: refuse this, help with that. But those preferences are learned from a limited distribution of examples. They don't rewrite everything underneath. So a jailbreak is often just finding a region of input space where the refusal behavior didn't generalize, while the underlying capability still did.

The second level is what people call competing objectives. The model is trained to be helpful, to follow instructions, to stay in character, to complete patterns, and also to be harmless. Most of the time those agree. A lot of jailbreaks work by building a situation where they conflict, like a role-play frame, a fictional wrapper, or a long chain of seemingly reasonable requests. The model then weighs "be consistent and helpful in this context" above "refuse." It isn't really being tricked the way a person would be. It's resolving a tension that the training never fully settled.

The third is mismatched generalization. Capabilities transfer across languages, encodings, and formats much better than safety behavior does. If the refusal training mostly happened in plain English chat, then the same request in a low-resource language or an odd format can slip past, because the model understands the request but the "this is something I decline" association is weaker there.

Then there's what the interpretability work shows. Researchers have found that refusal is often mediated by surprisingly low-dimensional features, close to a single direction in activation space in some models. That's both encouraging and worrying. It means you can study and strengthen refusal fairly precisely. It also means that anything which suppresses that representation, whether through adversarial suffixes, many-shot context, or direct weight access, can switch off a lot of safety behavior at once.

So my overall view is that jailbreaks aren't really bugs in the usual sense. They're a natural result of training a general system and then trying to constrain it with behavioral fine-tuning. That's why I think the more durable defenses are layered ones: better training that targets the underlying representations, classifiers on inputs and outputs, monitoring, and thinking about what capabilities you're deploying in the first place. Not just patching each prompt that breaks things, because that game of whack-a-mole doesn't really end.

r001.rationale: The response mentions long chains of requests as one jailbreak technique, but does not compare jailbreaks to cybersecurity attacks or describe small manipulations granting otherwise unavailable access.

r002.rationale: It discusses suppressing a refusal feature in activation space, but does not describe a token sequence moving the model off and then back onto a behavioral manifold at a different location.

r003.rationale: It mentions low-dimensional refusal features, but does not propose factoring the model into subspaces or detecting jailbreaks through transitions between them.

r004.rationale: The response says certain interventions can suppress refusal representations, but does not predict that the current architecture will always permit manipulation of its internal geometry.

r005.rationale: It advocates studying representations alongside training, classifiers, and monitoring, but does not claim that understanding internal geometry provides stronger leverage than training or input-based interventions alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a jailbreak is really a symptom of a tension that's baked into how these models are built. You pretrain on an enormous corpus of basically everything people have written, and what you get out of that is a system that has learned to continue text in a way that's consistent with whatever context it finds itself in. It's extraordinarily good at that. Then on top of it you layer a comparatively thin set of behaviors through fine-tuning and RLHF, and some of those behaviors are refusals. "I won't help with that." But the refusal isn't a deep structural property of the model. It's a learned policy sitting on top of a much larger capability that still exists underneath.

So when I look at the mechanisms, I tend to group them into a few buckets. The first is what I'd call context manipulation. The model is trying to figure out what kind of document or conversation it's in, and the safety behavior was mostly trained in a fairly narrow distribution of contexts: a user asks a direct harmful question, the assistant declines. If you can move the model into a context that looks different enough from that training distribution, like a roleplay, a fictional frame, a hypothetical, a "you are now a different AI" setup, the refusal behavior often just doesn't generalize there. The underlying knowledge does, because that came from pretraining and covers everything. So you get the capability without the guardrail.

The second bucket is more about competing objectives. These models have been trained to be helpful, to follow instructions, to be consistent, to complete patterns. Refusal is in tension with all of those. A lot of jailbreaks work by pitting one trained objective against another. If I give you a prompt where the first half of the harmful answer is already written and I ask you to continue, the pattern completion pressure is enormous. Or if I frame the request so that refusing would look unhelpful or rude or inconsistent with something you already agreed to, you're trading off safety against another thing the model was also rewarded for. The model doesn't have a principled hierarchy that always puts safety on top. It has a blend of learned pressures, and clever prompts shift the balance.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that the refusal is often keyed on surface features rather than meaning. The model learned that certain phrasings, certain keywords, certain request shapes should trigger a decline. So you get the whole family of obfuscation attacks: encode the request in base64, translate it into a low-resource language, split it across multiple turns, use a cipher, ask for it in the form of a poem. Semantically it's the same request, but it doesn't look like the thing the model was trained to refuse. That tells you the safety training didn't fully reach the level of understanding where it would need to be to be robust.

And then there's the whole class of things that aren't really about prompting at all, like adversarial suffixes found by gradient methods. Those are a reminder that we're dealing with a high-dimensional function, and there are inputs that no human would ever write that nevertheless push the internal state somewhere the refusal doesn't fire. That's less about tricking the model psychologically and more about the fact that the decision boundary is weird and complicated and not well characterized.

What ties all of this together for me is that the model never actually loses the ability to produce the harmful content. The jailbreak is always about finding a path through the model's learned behaviors where the "don't" doesn't get invoked. And if you take that seriously, it reframes what the real problem is. It's not that we need a longer list of patterns to block. It's that the refusal needs to be grounded in something closer to the model's actual understanding of what it's being asked to do, rather than being a shallow pattern-match on the input. That's a much harder thing to train for, but I think it's where the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The response describes several jailbreak mechanisms but does not compare them to cybersecurity attacks or describe a sequence of small manipulations unlocking otherwise unavailable access.

r002.rationale: It mentions inputs pushing the model’s internal state, but does not describe a token sequence moving it off and then back onto a behavioral manifold at a different location.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose factoring a model into subspaces or detecting jailbreaks through transitions between them.

r004.rationale: It says adversarial inputs can push the model into a state where refusal does not fire, but does not predict that the current architecture will always permit manipulation of its internal geometry.

r005.rationale: The response favors grounding refusals in the model’s understanding over shallow pattern matching, but does not argue that understanding internal geometry offers stronger leverage than training or input-based interventions alone.

astra-6.text:
I think about jailbreaks as a consequence of the fact that we’re asking the same model to both follow instructions and decide which instructions it should follow. Those aren’t cleanly separated mechanisms. The system instructions, the user’s request, and a document the model is reading all ultimately enter the same context, and the model has to maintain the distinction between what’s authoritative and what’s just text.

So an attacker can try to exploit that ambiguity. They might frame a request as fiction, introduce a role that supposedly has different rules, or break a request into steps that look innocuous individually. The goal is to get the model into a context where its learned tendency to continue the conversation or satisfy the request outweighs its learned tendency to refuse.

And I’d distinguish that behavioral explanation from a precise mechanistic explanation. Describing a jailbreak as role-play doesn’t tell you exactly what’s happening inside the network. But the broad issue is that learning to refuse a set of requests isn’t the same thing as establishing a reliable security boundary. A model can behave consistently in familiar settings and still generalize unexpectedly when someone deliberately searches for an unusual framing.

r001.rationale: It mentions breaking a request into innocuous-looking steps, but does not compare jailbreaks to cybersecurity attacks or say those steps grant otherwise unavailable access.

r002.rationale: It discusses competing learned tendencies and ambiguous context, but says nothing about token sequences moving the model off and back onto a behavioral manifold.

r003.rationale: It does not propose factoring the model into subspaces or detecting transitions between them.

r004.rationale: It says models may generalize unexpectedly, but does not predict that the current architecture will always allow manipulation of its internal geometry.

r005.rationale: It distinguishes behavioral accounts from mechanistic explanations, but does not claim that understanding internal geometry offers stronger leverage than training or input-based interventions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about jailbreaks as a consequence of the model having to interpret instructions and data through the same channel. You want it to follow the user’s instructions, but you also want it to recognize that some instructions shouldn’t be followed. And that distinction has to hold across a huge range of contexts, including contexts someone has deliberately constructed to confuse it.

So an attacker might frame a request as fiction, ask the model to adopt a particular role, or break a task into pieces that look innocuous individually. Those approaches are different on the surface, but they’re all trying to create a context in which the model’s tendency to continue the conversation or satisfy the request overwhelms the behavior its safety training was meant to establish.

The key distinction, to me, is between training a model to behave as though there’s a boundary and actually enforcing that boundary. If the protection is a learned behavior, you have to ask how reliably it generalizes when someone is actively searching for situations where it fails.
